Diversity and prevalence of Bartonella species in small mammals from Slovakia, Central Europe
Eva Špitalská1 & Lenka Minichová1 & Elena Kocianová1 & Ľudovít Škultéty1 & Lenka Mahríková2 & Zuzana Hamšíková2 & Mirko Slovák2 & Mária Kazimírová2
Received: 15 June 2017 /Accepted: 15 September 2017
$©$ Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany 2017

Abstract Wild-living rodents are important hosts for zoonotic pathogens. Bartonella infections are widespread in rodents; however, in Slovakia, knowledge on the prevalence of these bacteria in small mammals is limited. We investigated the prevalence and diversity of Bartonella species in the spleens of 640 rodents of six species (Apodemus flavicollis, Apodemus sylvaticus, Myodes glareolus, Microtus arvalis, Microtus subterraneus, and Micromys minutus) and in the European mole (Talpa europaea) from three different habitat types in south-western and central Slovakia. Overall, the prevalence of Bartonella spp. in rodents was $6 4 . 8 \%$ ; a rate of $7 3 . 8 \%$ was found in natural habitat (deciduous forest), $5 6 . 0 \%$ in suburban forest park and $6 4 . 9 \%$ in rural habitat. Bartonella spp. were detected in $6 3 . 0 \%$ of A. flavicollis, $69 \%$ of My. glareolus and $6 1 . 1 \%$ of M. arvalis and in T. europaea. However, Bartonella were not found in the other examined rodents. Molecular analyses of the 16S–23S rRNA intergenic spacer region revealed the presence of four different Bartonella spp. clusters. We identified B. taylorii, B. rochalimae, B. elizabethae, B. grahamii and Bartonella sp. wbs11 in A. flavicollis and My. glareolus. Bartonella genotypes ascribed to B. taylorii and B. rochalimae were found in M. arvalis. B. taylorii was identified in T. europaea. Questing Ixodes ricinus ticks that

were collected at the study sites were not infected with Bartonella. This study improves our understanding of the ecoepidemiology of Bartonella spp. in Europe and underlines the necessity for further research on Bartonella-host-vector associations and their consequences on animal and human health in Slovakia.
Keywords Bartonella $\cdot$ Rodents $\cdot$ Slovakia
Introduction

Bartonella, previously known as Grahamella (Birtles et al. 1995), are Gram-negative bacteria of medical and veterinary importance that belong to the class of alpha-proteobacteria. They infect the erythrocytes and endothelial cells of mammals and are adapted to distinct mammalian hosts. Bartonella are transmitted by ectoparasitic arthropods, although knowledge of their vectors is not well understood (Regier et al. 2016). Several blood-feeding arthropods, such as sand flies, human body lice, fleas, vole ear mites and ticks have been implicated in Bartonella transmission (Breitschwerdt and Kordick 2000). Some species of Bartonella (e.g. B. henselae, B. elizabethae, B. alsatica, B. vinsonii subsp. arupensis, B. bacilliformis, B. quintana, B. grahamii and B. washoensis) have been associated with human diseases with presentations that range from subclinical and self-limiting infection to severe, lifethreatening disease and have an increased risk of infection in immunocompromised patients (Breitschwerdt and Kordick 2000; Mogollon-Pasapera et al. 2009; Mosepele et al. 2012; Regier et al. 2016). Clinical studies have supported the transmission of Bartonella by ticks to humans (Morozova et al. 2005; Billeter et al. 2008, 2012).

Information (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). Bartonella phylogeny, which is based on a genome-wide dataset, has revealed four lineages. During evolution, these lineages have adapted to a variety of hosts and developed virulence factors associated with a diverse set of symptoms (Mullins et al. 2017). In contrast to the ancestral lineage 1, lineages 2, 3 and 4 comprise species isolated from various hosts. While the species of lineage 2 are limited to ruminant hosts and have an overlapping host range, the diversification of lineages 3 and 4 appear to result from the adaptation to distinct mammalian hosts (including voles, mice, rats, red squirrels, cats, dogs, foxes, rabbits and humans). Taxa of lineage 4 comprise a wide range of divergently adapted species that are frequently found in freeliving host populations. In contrast, the taxa of lineage 3, except for B. clarridgeiae, were sampled at a low prevalence (Engel et al. 2011).

Several Bartonella species have been detected in rodents from various regions worldwide (Gutiérrez et al. 2015). Among them, B. elizabethae, B. tribocorum, B. grahamii, B. vinsonii subsp. arupensis and B. washoensis have been associated with human infections (Daly et al. 1993; Welch et al. 1999; Kosoy et al. 2003, 2010). These findings underline the importance of understanding the reservoir competence of rodents for Bartonella, which is limited in Slovakia.

The yellow-necked mouse, Apodemus flavicollis (Melchior, 1834), and the bank vole, Myodes glareolus (Schreber, 1780), belong to predominantly occurring wild-living rodents in Slovakia. The striped field mouse, Apodemus agrarius (Pallas, 1771), is found primarily in the eastern part of the country. These rodents have a small home range and a relatively short lifespan. Apodemus spp., Microtus spp. and My. glareolus are hosts to ectoparasitic arthropods that play important roles in the maintenance and circulation of tick-borne microbial agents, such as Borrelia burgdorferi s.l., Borrelia miyamotoi, Anaplasma/ Ehrlichia, Rickettsia spp., Babesia microti and Candidatus Neoehrlicha mikurensis (Rizzoli et al. 2014). In Slovakia, the reservoir competence of wild-living rodents has been identified for several tick-borne zoonotic pathogens, i.e. Borrelia afzelii (Hanincová et al. 2003), Cand. Neoehrlichia mikurensis (Blaňarová et al. 2016; Hamšíková Svitálková et al. 2016), Babesia microti (Blaňarová et al. 2016; Hamšíková et al. 2016), and Borrelia miyamotoi (Hamšíková et al. 2017). However, the reservoir role of rodents for rickettsiae (Minichová et al. 2017) and the role of ticks as Bartonella vectors have not been identified.

Šebek (1960, 1975) was the first to report Bartonella infections in rodents in former Czechoslovakia. Bartonella sp. belonging to lineage 3 was identified by molecular methods in the spleen of an A. flavicollis female from central Slovakia in 2006 (Špitalská et al. 2008). Furthermore, Karbowiak et al. (2009) detected Bartonella in erythrocytes in Giemsa-stained

blood smears of A. agrarius from two sites in eastern Slovakia. Recently, Kraljik et al. (2016) ascribed Bartonella genotypes in A. agrarius from eastern Slovakia to B. grahamii, B. taylorii, B. birtlesii, B. clarridgeiae/B. rochalimae and B. elizabethae/B. tribocorum. Despite these studies, Bartonella epidemiology and host-vector associations in Central Europe, including Slovakia, are not well understood.

The present study analyses the prevalence and diversity of Bartonella spp. in small mammals from three ecologically distinct habitats of south-western and central Slovakia. The presence of Bartonella was examined in rodents as well as in questing Ixodes ricinus (L., 1758) to determine the role of ticks in transmission.
Materials and methods
Small mammals and ticks

Small mammals were live-trapped at three sites in Slovakia. The two sites, Bratislava (202–334 m above sea level, asl), which represents a suburban forest park with significant anthropogenic impact, and Fúgelka ( $3 3 6 { \mathrm { - } } 4 3 6 { \mathrm { ~ m } }$ asl), which comprises a non-fragmented deciduous forest, are located in the Small Carpathian Mountains (south-western Slovakia). The mountains have densely forested regions that are dominated by sessile oak (Quercus petraea) and European hornbeam (Carpinus betulus) at lower altitudes and European beech (Fagus sylvatica) at higher altitudes. The Bratislava and Fúgelka study sites were described in detail by Kazimírová et al. (2016). The third site, Prievidza (central Slovakia; 289 m asl), is near a settlement and represents a forest-steppe rural area with Carpathian oak-hornbeam forests (Berthová et al. 2016).

A total of 640 rodents comprising six species (A. flavicollis, wood mouse Apodemus sylvaticus (L., 1758), My. glareolus, common vole Microtus arvalis (Pallas, 1778), European pine vole Microtus subterraneus (de Selys-Longchamps, 1836), and Eurasian harvest mouse Micromys minutus (Pallas, 1771)) were live-trapped from April–July and September– October 2012–2014 by Sherman live traps baited with oat flakes (for details, see Svitálková et al. 2015 and Minichová et al. 2017). Captured rodents were transported to the laboratory, anaesthetized and sacrificed humanely according to the current laws of the Slovak Republic. A fresh intact corpse of a European mole Talpa europaea L., 1758 was found in the suburban forest park in June 2012. Spleen tissue samples were obtained from each animal and stored in $70 \%$ ethanol for DNA extraction.
In addition, 5767 questing I. ricinus, including 4795 nymphs and 972 adults, were collected by dragging the vegetation in Bratislava and Fúgelka. The ticks were stored in

$70 \%$ ethanol and subsequently identified by species, developmental stage and sex (see Svitálková et al. 2015). A selection of 1335 questing ticks (194 nymphs, 191 females and 90 males from Bratislava; 292 nymphs, 278 females and 290 males from Fúgelka) in pools of 3–7 samples were screened for the presence of Bartonella.
Molecular analysis

DNA samples from rodent spleens and questing ticks were used from previous studies (Svitálková et al. 2015; Minichová et al. 2017). We used PCR to determine if Bartonella DNA was present in individual rodent spleen samples and pooled tick samples. The 16S–23S rRNA intergenic spacer region (ITS) was amplified, generating a 420–780 bp product (Maggi et al. 2006). PCR reactions were carried out in a total volume of $2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { l }$ containing $2 ~ \mu \mathrm { l }$ of DNA template, $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { l }$ of Master mix (SuperHot PCR Master Mix, Bioron, Germany), $0 . 2 ~ \mu \mathrm { l }$ of each primer $( 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { l }$ of $1 0 0  { \mathrm { ~ m M ~ M g C l } _ { 2 } }$ $\mathrm { M g C l } _ { 2 }$ and $7 . 1 ~ \mu 1$ of nuclease free water. Amplification was performed in a thermocycler (Labcycler, SensoQuest, Germany). The thermal cycle reaction consisted of an initial 2 min denaturation at $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , followed by 40 cycles at $9 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 s, $6 6 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 s and $7 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 s, with a final extension at $7 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5 min. Positive and negative controls consisted of Bartonella DNA from infected rodents confirmed by sequencing and sterile water, respectively, and were used in each PCR reaction. PCR products were visualised on $1 \%$ agarose gels stained with GelRed Nucleic Acid Gel Stain (Biotium, Hayward, Canada). Bartonella-positive amplicons were purified and then analysed by sequencing in both directions with the same primers as for PCR amplification by Macrogen Inc. (Amsterdam, The Netherlands). DNA sequences were compared with those available in GenBank using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) (http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). The new sequences were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers MF039545- MF039578. A phylogenetic tree was constructed using the neighbour-joining method (Saitou and Nie 1987). Phylogenetic analysis was conducted using MEGA5 software (Tamura et al. 2011).
Statistical analysis

Statistical analyses to test for differences in the prevalence of bartonellae in rodents between years, seasons and sites were carried out using Fisher’s exact test with an online calculator (http://www.socscistatistics.com). A $p$ value $< 0 . 0 5$ was considered significant. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using an online calculator (http:// epitools.ausvet.com.au).
Results
Prevalence of Bartonella species

DNA of Bartonella spp. was not confirmed in any of the questing I. ricinus samples. In contrast, out of 641 small mammals represented by seven species, Bartonella DNA was detected in the spleens of 415 animals, including the European mole. The overall infection rate in rodents was $6 4 . 8 \%$ $9 5 \%$ CI 61.1–68.5), and ranged from $5 6 . 0 \%$ $9 5 \%$ $9 5 \% \mathrm { C I } 5 0 . 2 – 6 1 . 7 )$ in the suburban habitat to $7 3 . 8 \%$ $9 5 \%$ CI 68.7–78.8) in the nonfragmented forest (Table 1). Bartonella spp. were detected in $6 3 . 0 \%$ ( $9 5 \%$ CI 58.2–67.9) of A. flavicollis, $6 9 . 0 \%$ $9 5 \%$ CI 63.0–74.9) of My. glareolus and $6 1 . 1 \%$ $9 5 \% \mathrm { C I } 3 8 . 6 { - 7 9 . 7 } )$ $9 5 \%$ of M. arvalis. We found a significant difference in the bacterial prevalence between the Bratislava and Fúgelka sites $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ . Due to the small number of samples from 2013, we only investigated differences in prevalence between 2012 and 2014. The difference in Bartonella prevalence between 2012 and 2014 was significant in Bratislava $( p = 0 . 0 0 3 3 )$ ) but not in Fúgelka $( p = 0 . 5 4 5 6 )$ ). We detected an increase in Bartonella-positive rodents in autumn $8 6 . 1 \%$ ; $9 5 \%$ CI 82.3–89.8) compared to spring $4 1 . 6 \%$ ; $9 5 \%$ CI 36.0–47.1) (Table 2), and this difference between seasons was significant $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ .
Diversity of Bartonella in small mammals

Sequence analysis of the 16S–23S rRNA intergenic spacer region in 153 randomly selected spleen DNA lysates showed that the Bartonella strains detected among the investigated rodents, and the European mole belonged to multiple clusters, including B. taylorii, B. grahamii, B. elizabethae, Bartonella sp. wbs11 and B. rochalimae. Bartonella spp. in rodents from Fúgelka and Prievidza belonged to four different clusters and thus were more diverse than in the small mammals from Bratislava, where only two clusters (B. taylorii and B. rochalimae) were detected. The majority of DNA sequences were ascribable to B. taylorii (Fig. 1). Sequences from this study and their GenBank Accession numbers are given in Table S1.

Forty-eight sequences derived from spleen samples of small mammals trapped in Bratislava (A. flavicollis: 12 males, 13 females; My. glareolus: 10 males, 12 females; 1 T. europaea), 70 sequences from Fúgelka (A. flavicollis: 22 males, 13 females; My. glareolus: 16 males, 14 females; M. arvalis: 4 females, 1 male) and 12 sequences from Prievidza (A. flavicollis: 3 males, 5 females; My. glareolus: 1 male, 3 females) were identified as B. taylorii. Identities of these sequences ranged from 90 to $100 \%$ of bacterial sequences (GenBank Acc. Nos AJ269788, AJ269784) were previously identified in rodents from the United Kingdom (Birtles et al. 2000).

text: Discussion

Ectoparasitic arthropods and small mammals play important roles in the circulation of Bartonella species in Europe (Regier et al. 2016). Here, we detected the presence of Bartonella in small mammals from three habitat types in south-western and central Slovakia, but failed to detect bacteria in questing I. ricinus ticks.

The role of ticks in the epidemiology of Bartonella is unclear (Harrison et al. 2012; Regier et al. 2016; Silaghi et al. 2016), although experimental vector competence studies have demonstrated the transmission of B. henselae and B. birtlesii by I. ricinus ticks (Cotté et al. 2008; Reis et al. 2011). Our findings are supported by studies conducted in Sweden, Great Britain, Hungary, central Slovakia, Germany, Finland and Serbia, where Bartonella was not detected in questing ticks (Billeter et al. 2008; Špitalská et al. 2008; Schorn et al. 2011; Sormunen et al. 2016; Potkonjak et al. 2016). In contrast, up to $60 \%$ prevalence of Bartonella was detected in questing I. ricinus from particular sites in Europe (Regier et al. 2016). Moreover, Bartonella has been detected in engorged ticks from different hosts. For example, Lipatova et al. (2015) identified B. grahamii in I. ricinus larvae that were feeding on small mammals in Lithuania. Recently, Regier et al. (2017) showed that I. ricinus ticks that were removed from cats were positive for B. henselae DNA. These results indicate that ticks become infected by feeding on infected hosts and that pathogens can survive within ticks, but do not prove that ticks can transmit the infection to a mammalian host. Thus, further research is necessary to elucidate the role of ticks in the transmission of Bartonella spp. Rudolf et al. (2016) also highlighted the necessity to extend the list of haematophagous arthropods that are involved in Bartonella transmission, as they have demonstrated infection of sheep keds (Diptera) with B. melophagi .

Relatively high infection rates (from $2 5 \%$ to over $80 \%$ ) and a great diversity of Bartonella spp. have been reported in wildliving small rodent populations worldwide (Gutiérrez et al. 2015). In our study, Bartonella infection was demonstrated in $6 4 . 8 \%$ of examined rodents. This percentage is similar to levels reported from the United Kingdom $62 \%$ ; Birtles et al. 1994) and Germany $6 5 . 8 \%$ ; Silaghi et al. 2016) but is higher than the rates found in other European sites, e.g. $2 5 \%$ in Great Britain (Baker 1974; Healing 1981), $2 5 \mathrm { - } 3 1 \%$ in Poland (Bajer

et al. 2001; Pawełczyk et al. 2004; Welc-Falęciak et al. 2008), $2 7 - 2 8 \%$ in Denmark (Engbaek and Lawson 2004) and Spain (Maggi et al. 2009; Gil et al. 2010), $30 \%$ in Greece (Tea et al. 2004), $4 0 . 4 \%$ in Slovenia (Knap et al. 2007) and $3 0 { - } 5 6 . 4 \%$ in France (Gundi et al. 2004; Buffet et al. 2012). In contrast, a Bartonella prevalence rate of over $80 \%$ was detected in rodents in southern China and northern USA (Ying et al. 2002; Bai et al. 2011).

In addition to spatial variations, interspecific differences and temporal changes in Bartonella prevalence have been observed in rodents (Wiger 1979; Bajer et al. 2001; Karbowiak et al. 2005). In our study, the highest total prevalence was detected in My. glareolus $( 6 9 . 0 \% )$ and the lowest was in M. arvalis $( 6 1 \% )$ , although the values differed between sites and years (see Table 1). The range of interspecific variation in Bartonella spp. prevalence may be even greater, as demonstrated in rodents from Poland $( 7 - 6 6 \% )$ (Karbowiak et al. 2005) and Norway $( 1 0 - 3 2 \% )$ (Wiger 1979). These findings suggest that prevalence data may be affected by the density and dynamics of the rodent populations as well as by the numbers of examined animals belonging to a particular species. Furthermore, seasonal changes in Bartonella prevalence have also been registered. For example, Pawełczyk et al. (2004) found that Bartonella infections in the blood of M. arvalis in Poland were rare in the spring but were common in summer and autumn. Similar results were obtained in our study, i.e. a higher prevalence of infection was recorded in autumn than in spring. This seasonal difference was not detected at the rural site in Prievidza $( p = 1 . 0 )$ , which may be due to the low sample size.

Rodent-associated Bartonella species are genetically diverse (Gutiérrez et al. 2015; Regier et al. 2016). The Bartonella spp. present in the rodents and European mole investigated in this study were found to belong to multiple groups, including B. taylorii, B. grahamii, B. elizabethae, Bartonella sp. wbs11 and B. rochalimae. These species were clustered into phylogenetic lineages 3 and 4 and were also confirmed in A. agrarius from eastern Slovakia (Kraljik et al. 2016). Likewise, Buffet et al. (2012) detected different Bartonella genotypes that were related to three known species (B. taylorii, B. grahamii and B. doshiae) and two unidentified Bartonella species that were associated with rodents in France. B. taylorii, B. grahamii and B. rochalimae were also found in rodents in Lithuania (Lipatova et al. 2015) and uncultured Bartonella sp., B. grahamii, B. taylorii and Bartonella sp. N40 were detected in rodents from Germany (Silaghi et al. 2016).

In this study, the majority of sequences derived from rodent spleens $(8 5 \% )$ were ascribable to B. taylorii. This species causes infection in animals, although its real pathogenic potential is unknown (Lipatova et al. 2015). We expected to find B. taylorii and detected it in A. flavicollis, My. glareolus, M. arvalis and T. europaea. Previously, B. taylorii was

isolated from My. glareolus in the United Kingdom (Bown et al. 2004) and Siberia (Jiyipong et al. 2014) and was detected in A. sylvaticus, A. agrarius, A. uralensis (Pallas, 1811), A. witherbyi (Thomas, 1902), M. minutus, Microtus agrestis (L., 1761), Microtus spp. and Mus domesticus L., 1758 in Austria (Schmidt et al. 2014), Lithuania (Lipatova et al. 2015), Sweden (Holmberg et al. 2003), Spain (Gil et al. 2010) and Greece (Tea et al. 2004).

Four sequences derived from A. flavicollis and My. glareolus in the Fúgelka natural habitat were found to be similar to B. grahamii, a causative agent of human renitis (Kerkhoff et al. 1999). B. grahamii was also isolated from a human patient in the USA in a region that is endemic to this pathogen (Eremeeva et al. 2007) and was found to infect different rodent species (A. sylvaticus, A. agrarius, A. uralensis, A. witherbyi, M. minutus, M. arvalis, M. agrestis and M. domesticus) (Mogollon-Pasapera et al. 2009; Oksi et al. 2013; Lipatova et al. 2015). Because of its worldwide occurrence and its prevalence in Slovakia, B. grahamii may represent a potential risk for human infection in this country.

We also detected B. elizabethae DNA in A. flavicollis. This result is surprising because this species is a human pathogen and has been associated with rats. It was described in 1993 in the USA, causes endocarditis and is transmitted by fleas (Mogollon-Pasapera et al. 2009). However, Kraljik et al. (2016) detected B. elizabethae in wild-living mice A. agrarius from eastern Slovakia. B. elizabethae was also cultivated from A. sylvaticus in Georgia (Malania et al. 2016). Although it is unlikely to represent a serious risk for the local human population, it should be considered a potential agent of infection to people in contact with rodents.

Fifteen sequences found primarily in A. flavicollis but also in M. arvalis were clustered into phylogenetic lineage 3 and showed identity to B. rochalimae, an infectious zoonotic agent. This species is associated with dogs and foxes (Engel et al. 2011), although it has been suggested that rodents are reservoirs for this pathogen (Lin et al. 2008). Our data support previous identifications of B. rochalimae in My. glareolus in Lithuania (Lipatova et al. 2015) and France (Buffet et al. 2012).

In conclusion, our study provides evidence that a high proportion of rodents from selected sites in south-western and central Slovakia harbour Bartonella, which can be transmitted to other hosts including humans. Thus, it is important to continue investigating Bartonella spp. that circulate in the wildlife to estimate potential risks for the Slovakian population that have contact with rodents. Small mammals and humans share the same environment and thus extensive surveillance should be performed, especially in areas where humans encounter small mammals.
